evidence.title: Informed Consent for Ambient Documentation Using Generative AI in Ambulatory Care
evidence.outcome: Clinician-reported barriers to explaining ambient AI during consent
evidence.effect: Clinicians reported time constraints, concerns about biased presentation, and uncertainty about which details to disclose; frequencies were not quantified.
evidence.quote: Clinicians cited time constraints, concerns about bias in presenting the technology, and uncertainty about what details to include ( Box 3 ).

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether training frontline staff improves their delivery of AI disclosures or their ability to answer patient questions about AI. One qualitative study of ambient AI consent (pmid:40694347) suggests that clinicians face time constraints and uncertainty about what to disclose, which shows that the problem exists but does not show that training fixes it.

perspectives.view: Three sources endorse the practice, and all three are frameworks or commentaries. No trial, cohort, or before-after study measures disclosure delivery, staff knowledge, or patient understanding after training. The one supplied study documents the hazard only. Under GRADE conventions, certainty for the practice itself cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In a real deployment of ambient AI in the United States, 18 clinicians and 103 patients took part. Clinicians reported time constraints, concerns about presenting AI in a biased way, and uncertainty about which details to disclose. The study did not count how often these occurred. Training alone may not address time pressure within the visit.

The reported barriers suggest that disclosure may be skipped or delivered inconsistently when visits run short. Some patients may then agree to AI use without understanding it. No study shows whether training reduces these missed or incomplete disclosures, so health systems would need to check disclosure completion themselves.

Patients in the ambient AI study depended on clinicians to explain the tool, and clinicians said they were unsure what to say. Such uncertainty may weaken patients' trust and their ability to ask informed questions. Whether trained staff answer patient questions more clearly has not been measured.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare trained and untrained staff, or measure before and after training, on disclosure completion rates, accuracy of answers to patient questions, patient comprehension, and visit time. They should also test whether short scripts or other workflow supports add to the effect of training when visits are short.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The single hazard study does not report whether its patients came from these groups. Training content and its effects on patients who need interpreters or plain-language explanations remain unexamined, and one endorsing commentary calls for consent tailored to literacy without supplying evidence on how to achieve it.
